narrative:
The model estimated a 50.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was denied. This is a probability, not a certainty, but it placed you on the failing side of the decision.

Your application was denied mainly because of the combined signal from three factors. The strongest factor was your family-income bracket. Being in the lower-middle income group actually pushed the prediction toward passing rather than failure, but that favorable effect was not enough to outweigh the academic concerns. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 24, it was well below the average of about 37 for accepted students, and it pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The third factor was your class-rank group in your third year: a decile of 2, compared with an accepted-student average near 5.8, also pushed toward failure. In practical terms, the model saw a relatively low LSAT score and low third-year class rank as strong warning signs, while your income background worked slightly in your favor.

To improve future applications, focus on the factors you can change. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, seek academic advising to strengthen your record, and ask admissions offices for individualized review. You may also provide context for your academic performance and ask whether conditional admission or a post-baccalaureate path is available.
